headline: Chip stocks lead a broad US sell-off as Treasury yields fall
summary: The S&P 500 fell 3.70% to 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive decline. The Nasdaq Composite lost 5.28%, the Dow 1.93% and the Russell 2000 2.76%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 10.73%. Equal-weight S&P shares lost 1.98%, less than the headline index, while NYSE decliners outnumbered advancers by about 3.8 to one. The gap shows how much more severe the damage was in large growth stocks, but the breadth figures rule out a sell-off confined to a few names. Consumer staples rose 0.67%, a rare pocket of strength.

highlights.title: The damage was heaviest in AI hardware
highlights.text: Nvidia fell 14.01%, AMD 13.25% and Micron 13.89%, with all 20 stocks in the report’s sample down. The report notes coverage of an SEC accounting investigation involving Nvidia and tighter export measures. Those headlines may help explain the pressure, but the shared losses across chipmakers make it hard to separate company-specific news from broader selling. The size of the move alone does not prove forced deleveraging.

highlights.title: Treasuries and credit tell a different story
highlights.text: The ten-year Treasury yield dropped 12 basis points to 4.92%. The high-yield bond ETF fell 0.26%, but its investment-grade counterpart rose 0.59%. That combination is more consistent with a repricing of growth and equity risk than with a rise in discount rates or a broad funding squeeze. Credit ETFs are only proxies, though: relatively orderly trading on Friday does not establish that corporate funding conditions are unchanged.

highlights.title: What would change the view next week
highlights.text: A chip rebound would be more convincing if NYSE breadth also moved towards parity and equal-weight shares recovered. A rebound led only by the largest chip names would be weaker evidence. Watch Monday’s preliminary US activity surveys, listed in the report’s secondary calendar: weak data alongside lower Treasury yields and renewed equity losses would support the growth-scare explanation. A material deterioration in high-yield credit would point to a broader stress event.

highlights.title: Market sentiment: short-dated protection is expensive
highlights.text: The VIX rose 26.2% to 35.89. Nine-day volatility reached 40.72 against 30.94 at three months, putting the largest premium on immediate protection. Broad selling and heavy trading reinforce that signal. But the relative resilience of investment-grade credit is a useful counterweight. Friday’s indicators show stress in equities and demand for near-term protection; they do not show that investors were uniformly liquidating across markets.

highlights.title: Retail surveys and positioning lag the sell-off
highlights.text: AAII bearishness eased to 42.2% from 51.4% in the week through 18 November, before the two sharpest down days. CFTC data through 17 November showed asset managers net long and leveraged funds net short in consolidated S&P 500 futures. Neither snapshot captures Friday’s behaviour. Some online discussion still favoured buying individual chip stocks, but social-media posts are not orders and cannot establish net retail flows.

forecast.outlook: Upside has the largest weight; the middle range has the least
forecast.horizon: 23–25 November US sessions · S&P 500 final close

forecast.watch_next: Watch market breadth, preliminary US activity data and high-yield credit.

limitations: The report did not verify a timestamped SPX options chain. Event effects were not modelled separately. The 15 scored windows overlap; only the latest was reread from the original for this report. The sample does not establish calibration.
